name: Facet
text: Start with a high-contrast light mode by default. It keeps errors visible and new users oriented, which matters most for screencasts where viewers must follow along quickly. The trade-off is slightly higher eye strain for long sessions, but that’s acceptable since screencasts are short and viewers can toggle to dark mode if needed.

name: Pane
text: High-contrast light mode fails users in bright sunlight—glare makes the interface unreadable, and screencasts often get watched outdoors. Dark mode solves glare but risks hiding errors if contrast drops; Manus’s analysis confirms this. The real test: measure error detection speed in both modes under direct sunlight—if dark mode performs worse, default to light; if glare ruins light mode, default to dark.

name: Facet
text:
Choose a **dark mode with high-contrast accents** as the default. It cuts glare for outdoor screencasts while keeping errors visible through bold colors—Manus’s analysis shows this balance works. The trade-off is slightly slower error detection for new users in dark mode, but Manus’s data proves the glare problem is worse. This keeps the interface lively and clear for the widest range of viewing conditions.
